title: How Erie, PA Brought ShotSpotter Back Using Public-Private Funding
summary: Grant funding ended and Erie's gunfire went unreported. Hear how local partners funded ShotSpotter's return and what the coverage gap revealed.
body_markdown:
When grant funding expired, Erie, Pennsylvania, lost its ShotSpotter coverage. Months later, local partners helped bring it back, establishing a public-private model for funding gunshot detection.


When ShotSpotter was deactivated, the gap was noticeable right away. Calls reporting gunfire declined, ShotSpotter alerts went silent, and much of the city's gunfire continued to go unreported. That’s when local businesses and nonprofit organizations stepped in, forming a public-private funding coalition that brought ShotSpotter back in August 2026 — all without using a single taxpayer dollar.


In the video below, Erie's police chief, mayor, and a city councilman explain how the public-private funding coalition came together and why restoring ShotSpotter mattered.


### Gunfire That Wasn’t Reported


One of the biggest lessons for Erie’s team was how much gunfire never reached 911. In the video, Chief Richard E. Lorah described a homicide that initially went unreported. The case began as a missing person investigation, and wasn’t identified as a homicide until well after the shooting.


ShotSpotter's location and acoustic data can help police determine when and where gunfire occurred. In this case, that gave investigators a starting point to review nearby home surveillance footage, uncover additional leads, and ultimately find video of the homicide. As Chief Lorah explained,


“That would have been an unsolved homicide. That would have been a cold case because we had no idea when the shooting took place.”


### How the Public-Private Funding Partnership Started


Mayor Daria Devlin explained that Erie is not in a strong financial position. Every dollar for public safety technology competes with other city priorities. The city first deployed ShotSpotter across a six-square-mile area under a two-year, $910,000 grant-funded contract. When that funding ended, the city had to find a different funding model.


Rather than asking community partners to address the city's broader financial challenges, Erie leaders made a specific case for supporting ShotSpotter. As Mayor Devlin explained, “It made sense for them to step up and say they can help with this one thing. We can’t help with everything, but this is one specific, clear item that we can help with.”


Local businesses, hospitals, and universities funded ShotSpotter’s return.


Building that coalition, helping them see the value and helping them see too that they’re helping us as a City, us as a public safety entity, that really made it clear to them why this was valuable for everyone.”


Daria Devlin


Mayor of Erie, PA


### Show Partners the Value


The pitch worked because it showed partners their own stake. Their contribution helped the city and the public safety agencies protecting their neighborhoods. That connection is what turned a budget problem into a shared project.


Erie's experience with ShotSpotter before its deactivation also helped demonstrate the technology's value. City Councilman Andre Horton pointed to at least two cases in which ShotSpotter played a key role in securing convictions: “A couple of incidents where ShotSpotter was very instrumental in bringing someone forward and holding them accountable, all the way to conviction. If something happened to my child in one of those situations, I would want every tool available at my disposal to bring the offender or the perpetrator forward to be held accountable.”
